abstract: Allele frequencies tracked through time, from ancient DNA, museum collections or monitoring, offer a direct view of selection. Their value depends on whether the sampling design can distinguish change caused by selection from genetic drift and from the noise of sampling few individuals, often sequenced at low coverage. Researchers need to know how much power a design has before committing specimens and sequencing effort, which usually requires study-specific simulations. We present SPOT (Selection Power Over Time), a browser-based simulator that estimates the power to detect directional selection at a candidate locus from samples taken at several dates. Users describe the sampling design (dates, number of individuals, sequencing depth) and a biological scenario (inheritance system, generation time, effective population size, starting allele frequency, selection coefficient and dominance). Within seconds, SPOT simulates selection while accounting for sampling, genotype calling and drift, and sets the detection threshold from simulations without selection. Its sample-size planner shows how many individuals are needed to reach a target power. Conventional approaches, which model sampling error but not drift, overestimate power when drift is strong: in a museum insect case study, a threshold ignoring drift reported 69% power but called 10% of neutral loci selected instead of 5%; the drift-aware threshold gave 55%. SPOT agreed with the individual-based simulator SLiM in allele-frequency distributions, power and false-positive rates. Case studies of museum insects and human ancient DNA show how SPOT identifies detectable selection coefficients and helps allocate specimens and sequencing effort. SPOT is open source and runs without installation.
